# `lemma_unproved`: a lemma whose theorem the checker could not prove

A lemma (`@[lemma]`) states a theorem `P` in its result type, `{Unit | P}`. Its body is the proof.
The checker proves `P` at every place the body can return, using what is known there:
- the branch of the `if` or `match` that leads to it;
- the facts from lemma calls before it;
- every `assert` before it that was itself proved.

If one of those returns does not prove, the lemma is **unproved**. A call to an unproved lemma
gives the caller no facts. Nothing is assumed on its word. This is a warning, and an error inside
a `cap verified` module.

An `assert` inside a lemma is a step of the proof, checked statically. It never runs. A step that
can't be proved is not assumed afterwards, so `assert false` cannot "prove" anything.

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  fn cat(xs : List(Int), ys : List(Int)) : List(Int) do
    match xs do
      Nil -> ys
      Cons(h, t) -> Cons(h, cat(t, ys))
    end
  end

  @[lemma]
  fn cat_nil(xs : List(Int)) : {Unit | cat(xs, Nil) == xs} do
    ()
  end

  fn main() : Int do
    0
  end
end
```

`cat(xs, Nil) == xs` is true, but proving it needs induction on `xs`. Unfolding `cat` once leaves
`cat(t, Nil)` in the goal, which is the same question one element shorter.

## The fix

Split the cases with `match`, and call the lemma itself on the tail. The recursive call is the
induction hypothesis. The checker accepts it because `cat_nil(t)` recurses on a smaller list, so
it terminates.

```march
mod Main do
  fn cat(xs : List(Int), ys : List(Int)) : List(Int) do
    match xs do
      Nil -> ys
      Cons(h, t) -> Cons(h, cat(t, ys))
    end
  end

  @[lemma]
  fn cat_nil(xs : List(Int)) : {Unit | cat(xs, Nil) == xs} do
    match xs do
      Nil -> ()
      Cons(_, t) -> cat_nil(t)
    end
  end

  fn main() : Int do
    0
  end
end
```

When a single step is still too big, state it as an `assert` before the return. The assert is
proved on its own, then used.

## Why the rule exists

A lemma never runs, so nothing at run time checks its theorem. Facts from an unproved lemma would
be assumptions without evidence, and one false assumption is enough to "prove" any refinement in
the program.

See also: [the language reference](../refinement-types.md), [the lemmas guide](../lemmas.md), `invalid_lemma`, `lemma_unproved_call`.
